title: The Only Question That Hasn't Needed an Answer for 2,400 Years
excerpt: Plato banished artists as makers of shadows. Today we buy them as an asset class. A journey through 24,236 fragments reveals: art needs no definition. It needs beholders.
content:
Ever since Plato banished painters from his Republic for merely imitating shadows, humanity has tortured itself with a question that is, frankly, absurd: What is art? 2,400 years later we still have no answer. And that, precisely, is the only consolation we have.

The Tyranny of Definition

The Latin ars simply means skill. A craft, a technique, the mastery of material. But for what? To make empires richer? To produce a beauty no one understands? Every epoch has offered its answer, and every one grew obsolete faster than the last.

The barbarians stood before Greek statues and saw genera of the divine. We stand before bananas taped to walls and see 120,000 US dollars. The concept of art does not shift through sudden enlightenment but through power and discourse. Who decides what art is? The curator with the documentary beard, the collector with the Panama hat, the algorithm — or the individual who stands in front of it and suddenly feels something they cannot name?

From Skill to Commerce

Works of art emerge at the end of a creative process — or they are the process itself, like performances that vanish into nothing, or process art that dissolves while you watch. New media, film, computers, the internet — all of them have blown the frame apart. Today, art means any human activity with a communicative or aesthetic purpose. That is wonderfully liberating and terribly unsettling. Because if everything can be art, then nothing is art anymore — except the price tag.

The Eternal Shift

The institutions claim they lead the discourse. Museums, galleries, biennials — together they dynamically define what is currently valid. But this shift is not progressive. It is circular. We are still negotiating the questions Plato posed in the cave: Is art a mirror of reality, or the creation of a new one? The answer: it is the mirror of our society, and our society is a hall of mirrors of capitalism.

24,236 Truths

Imagine taking a self-portrait apart into 24,236 individual pieces. Each fragment is a slice of one's own skin, one's own eyes, one's own colors. But viewed in isolation they are abstract. Meaningless. Free. You hold a piece of canvas in your hand, worth $77, or maybe $777, depending on how many brothers and sisters it still has.

The mechanic is simple and brutal: the fewer pieces available, the more expensive the remaining ones become. In the end, the least popular pictures will be the most expensive. Not because they are beautiful. Not because they make sense. But because they are scarce.

That is the joke the market doesn't get: value emerges from scarcity, not from meaning. But art was meant to be the place where meaning emerges — so that value could even exist. No art, no sense; no sense, no value. And yet capitalism flips the script. It turns the meaning-maker into a commodity, the mirror of society into an investment vehicle. It devours the world of sense along with the worth of things.

Laughter as a Declaration of Love

We love art because it is the only proof we have of free will. Nothing about a brushstroke is necessary, nothing evolutionary about a particular combination of colors. Art is pointless in the best possible sense — it exists beyond utility and purpose, beyond optimization and return. It is the artificial within the cultural context, the thing that allows us to interpret the world instead of merely consuming it.

And that is why all we can do now is laugh at the art world. I LAUGH YOU. It is a bitter laugh, the kind that catches in your throat when you watch fragments of a self-portrait turn into ETFs for aesthetes. Every piece carries the artist's DNA, but the buyer fills it with their own meaning. That is authentic. That is true. Sense lies not in the whole, not in the grand narrative, but in the details, in the individual little pieces of every consciousness.

The Answer That Isn't One

There is no universal definition of art. There are only 24,236 individual truths, 24,236 consciousnesses standing before a fragment, seeing something no one else sees. Whoever reduces reality to a simple common denominator loses exactly what gives it meaning.

Plato was wrong: painters do not paint shadows. They paint the only reality that counts — the subjective one. When we stop asking "What is art?", we begin to understand. Art is not what hangs in the museum. Art is what happens when you stand before a fragment — whether it costs $77 or $777 — and suddenly know that meaning cannot be bought, even if the scrap of paper can.

The only question that counts is not: What is art? But: What does it mean to you? And that answer is one only you can give — between the lines, beyond the price tag, in the free open space of laughter.
